channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Short-term versus chronic stress: How each one affects your body
item.description: Figuring out how stress affects your body can be a challenge because the answer depends on how stressed you are and for how long.

item.title: AHA: Discontinuing statins noninferior to continuation in older adults without known cardiovascular disease
item.description: It is generally safe for older adults without a history of cardiovascular disease to discontinue statins for primary prevention, according to a study published online Nov. 7 in the New England Journal of Medicine to coincide with the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026, held from Nov. 6 to 9 in Chicago.

item.title: Can a scent really sharpen your memory? It's complicated
item.description: The sense of smell shares an intimate but mysterious connection with memory. We know that past experiences can flash vividly to mind if we smell a scent that accompanied them. This has led to claims that aromatherapy can enhance memory or even diminish cognitive decline. But the mechanisms by which the brain associates experience with scent are still being unraveled, and there is mixed scientific evidence to back up such claims.

item.title: Air pollution exposure tied to atopic dermatitis in children
item.description: Air pollution exposure is associated with increased atopic dermatitis (AD) prevalence in children, according to a review published online Nov. 9 in JAMA Pediatrics.

item.title: RNA switch lets drugs control gene therapy protein production
item.description: Bioengineers at the University of California San Diego have developed a technology that allows drugs to control when cells produce therapeutic proteins, which could potentially make gene therapies safer and more adaptable for treating chronic diseases.

item.title: Personalized therapies for Crohn's and ulcerative colitis may follow from method that identifies harmful gut bacteria
item.description: Which gut bacteria contribute to the development or worsening of chronic inflammation? An international research team led by Dr. Lukas Mager from University Hospital Tübingen and Prof. Kathy McCoy from the University of Calgary has developed an approach to identify and selectively target such bacteria. The researchers identified two bacterial species that promote intestinal inflammation and compounds that selectively inhibit their growth. Published in the journal Gut, the study could pave the way for personalized therapies for inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

item.title: GLP-1s often contain untested additive combinations, study finds
item.description: Use of GLP-1 receptor agonist medications (GLP-1s) has skyrocketed in recent years, and many people are using "compounded" GLP-1 products: medicines that include GLP-1s as well as other active substances, some of which are not regulated by the FDA. A new study found that compounded GLP-1s now make up a large majority of weight-loss medicines, commonly containing vitamin B12 analogs that have not been tested for safety in combination with GLP-1s.

item.title: New body map traces origins of complex movements in the brains of mice
item.description: A new biological blueprint of how the body of a mouse is represented in its brain could help scientists answer a fundamental question: How do we perform complex motions that use more than one body part, such as coordinating arm, hand, head and lips to sip a spoonful of soup? The study was published in Nature Communications.

item.title: A microbe-made molecule may reverse gut damage by boosting NAD levels
item.description: Scientists at Rutgers Health have discovered a molecule produced by "good" gut bacteria that rapidly heals the intestinal lining, protecting against severe inflammatory diseases and triggering increased production of a coenzyme whose levels diminish with age.

item.title: Longer inhibitory connections can push simulated neural networks beyond critical tipping point
item.description: In neuroscience, the brain criticality hypothesis proposes that neurons in the brain are arranged in such a way that neural activity lies at or near a transition point between two extremes: an ordered state where neural activity dies out quickly and a disordered state where neural activity tends to spread quickly and potentially grow uncontrollably. This transition point is known as criticality, while the two activity regimes on either side of it are known as subcritical and supercritical, respectively.

item.title: AHA: More intensive blood pressure lowering cuts future cardiovascular risk after stroke, transient ischemic attack
item.description: For adults with previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, targeting a systolic blood pressure

item.title: Forever chemical disturbs early development in stem cell model
item.description: Research using stem cell-derived models of early human development suggests that PFOS, a persistent substance belonging to the PFAS group, can interfere with processes critical for early germ cell and embryonic development. The study, from Karolinska Institutet, is published in the journal Human Reproduction Open.

item.title: Blood NAD levels track heart disease, not aging, study of more than 1,000 adults finds
item.description: Vilnius University researchers find that whole-blood NAD levels remain stable with age in healthy men and increase slightly in women, but are lower in people with cardiovascular disease, particularly hypertension.

item.title: Petroleum-based lubricants linked to MS risk
item.description: A new study from Karolinska Institutet has shown that people with multiple sclerosis (MS) were more likely than people without the disease to report that they had been exposed to petroleum-based lubricants at work. The work is published in the journal Neurology.

item.title: Mapping an enzyme offers clues to treating rare genetic disease
item.description: Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have mapped an enzyme that could be targeted to develop new treatments for glutaric aciduria type 1 (GA1), a rare genetic disorder that can lead to brain damage, revealing new details about how the enzyme works and how its activity is controlled. The findings were published in Science Advances.

item.title: Some ketogenic diets found to cause mitochondrial stress and lead to inflammation
item.description: New University of Cincinnati Cancer Center research found that a ketogenic diet high in long-chain saturated fatty acids can increase inflammation.

item.title: Early changes linked to ovarian cancer may leave a trace in the blood—new study
item.description: The most common type of ovarian cancer tends to grow quickly. It's called high-grade serous ovarian cancer and often starts in a fallopian tube, one of the tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries toward the uterus.

item.title: Giving AI a 'childhood' offers insights into language development
item.description: Every parent has watched it happen, and no scientist can fully explain how. A baby enters the world unable to understand a single word. Within a few years, that child recognizes thousands of words, follows complex sentences and communicates their own thoughts.

item.title: Final trial results show promising long-term survival with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab in advanced thymic tumors
item.description: Final results from the phase 2 PECATI clinical trial demonstrate encouraging long-term survival outcomes with the combination of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab in patients with previously treated advanced B3-thymoma and thymic carcinoma.

item.title: Drug safety information must remain accessible as patients move from websites to AI
item.description: A prescription drug warning can be accurate and still be difficult for a patient to use. What matters is not only the information itself but also how and where people receive it. This becomes especially important as patients increasingly use AI systems to find answers about medications, sometimes without visiting the original source.

item.title: Congenital syphilis rates soared in US newborns from 2012 to 2022
item.description: Congenital syphilis rates among U.S. newborns increased nearly sixfold from 2012 to 2022, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. The data show rising rates across all demographics and income levels, with the sharpest increases among Native Americans.

item.title: Blocking excess scarring helps prevent heart failure development
item.description: Most heart failure cases are caused to a large degree by a buildup of excess scar tissue in the heart, which currently has no treatments. Now, researchers have successfully prevented the development of severe heart failure in a mouse model of heart attack by blocking a protein that triggers the formation of excessive scar tissue.

item.title: Precision RNA therapy offers hope for brain receptor disorders
item.description: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Academia Sinica in Taiwan have developed an experimental RNA-based treatment that prevents brain damage and improves learning, memory and social behavior in mice carrying a rare genetic mutation associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.

item.title: Study measures impact of pandemic stress on gun violence spike
item.description: The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with one of the most dramatic swings in homicide in modern American history.

item.title: Survey on COVID-19 smell loss reveals over 50% of respondents still have symptoms after 5 years
item.description: Since the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers at Virginia Commonwealth University's School of Medicine have maintained a national database of patients affected by COVID-19-related smell loss. Their latest survey shows that more than half of respondents are still impacted by smell dysfunction five years after initial infection.

item.title: Engineered hydrogel could make testicular reconstruction feel more natural
item.description: Researchers at UBC's Okanagan and Vancouver campuses are developing a softer testicular implant that could offer patients a more natural feel following surgical reconstruction.

item.title: Measles elimination at risk—and what a Florida study shows about Pfizer's COVID vaccine
item.description: A Florida study comparing deaths after the Pfizer and Moderna COVID vaccines is getting a lot of attention, and one statistic from it is filling the echo chambers: a 40% higher rate of death with Pfizer. This edition closes with a closer look at that number and why it doesn't show that the vaccine caused deaths.

item.title: Brain atlas reveals how aging unfolds differently across brain regions, cell types and sexes
item.description: How do we age, and how do we become more at risk of brain diseases as we age? An Arizona State University-led team is helping answer those questions with a new high-resolution atlas of the aging primate brain.

item.title: Intensified liver-directed radionuclide therapy shows promise for patients with metastatic neuroendocrine tumors
item.description: Combining intraarterial and intravenous administration of peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) can selectively intensify treatment for liver-dominant metastatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) while still effectively delivering treatment throughout the whole body. This hybrid approach safely delivered over three times more radiation directly to liver metastases, resulting in encouraging tumor responses among patients. This research was published online in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine.

item.title: Where will Ebola spread next? Travel patterns offer clues
item.description: How many trips have you squeezed into the past 10 days? Whether you're in Boston or across the globe, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, your daily routine keeps you on the move. Between seven work commutes, a couple of grocery runs, a pharmacy stop and weekend dinner with friends, you can cover a lot of ground.
